answer: The classical transform has Theta(log n) levels, and each level has to bring the partners of every butterfly together and then combine them. On a tape machine each level is one sequential pass over all Theta(n) stored bits, so the levels together cost Theta(n log n). That is why the classical approach alone suggests n log n. The new algorithm looks for savings in two places, and it needs both at once. First, movement: swapping two address chunks of u bits in one operation costs O(V u^tau) with a fixed tau < 1, so many address bits move at once instead of one level at a time. Second, arithmetic: one round of butterfly steps across up to d axes runs as a single pass in O(V d^lambda') with lambda' < 1, instead of d separate passes. A layout first gathers the bits of the axes so that many levels become one such round. The per-level cost then drops below a full pass because the recursion's branching ratio s/W is below m, which gives a power-saving exponent. The savings are all powers of the logarithm, so the single machine runs in O(n (lg n)^(1-kappa)) with kappa = 2^-182, which is o(n log n). Confidence is moderate to high on this outline. I followed the cited arguments but did not check the exponent margin arithmetic beyond the cited formulas, and I did not open the algebra pages behind the rank count s < Wm.

citations.quote: On a tape machine that is one pass over the whole stored volume of $\Theta(n)$ bits per level, so the levels cost $\Theta(n\log n)$.
Interchanging two address chunks of $u$ bits moves $u$ address bits at once for $O(Vu^\tau)$ with fixed $\tau<1$
The [sifigeg](tiz) does one round of butterflies on up to $d$ axes at once for $O(Vd^{\lambda'})$ with $\lambda'<1$, instead of $d$ separate passes.
A tape machine performs one butterfly factor per whole-array pass, so $D$ separate factors would require $D$ whole-array passes
So any fixed $\tau<1$ with $s/W<m^\tau$ gives $\mathcal C(f)=O(f^\tau)$, and an interchange costs $O(Vf^\tau)$.
If $s=Wm$, depth $j$ contributes $m^j$, the sum is about $f$, and the cost is proportional to $Vf$: no saving.

key_idea.statement: A tape machine pays one full pass per butterfly level, so the way below n log n is to make one pass do the work of many levels, which needs both cheaper address movement and cheaper arithmetic.
key_idea.quote: The remedy is to let one pass do the work of many levels, which needs cheaper movement and cheaper arithmetic together

stuck.note: The formula is clear, but the page never says why this two-point step is called a butterfly or how it relates to the transform in the question. I got past it by guessing it is the usual butterfly of the transform.

I followed that the smallest of the seven margins fixes the saving and that kappa is half of it. I did not check the other six margins, and I could not see why splitting the margin in half is the right allowance for the logarithm factors.

reason: Answered with moderate to high confidence on the core outline. I read 10 of 15 pages: nut, kaf, tiz, mov, pid, rut, fam, vor, reb and dol. The n log n cost comes from Theta(log n) levels, each one full pass over Theta(n) bits, and the savings come from chunk interchange and multi-axis butterfly rounds with exponents below 1. Not opened and not needed for the answer: the Sikusup and chirp pages, the Gepupog frame page, and the katisen page. Some margin arithmetic and the rank count were accepted from the cited formulas rather than checked.
